sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

sections.title: Start
sections.content: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration Ting-Hsuan Chen1 Louison Lu1 Jiaheng Luo1 Henghui Bao1 Yiyu Chen2 Quan Nguyen1 Yue Wang1 Siheng Zhao1 Han Jiang1 Qi Pan1 1University of Southern California Equal contribution Corresponding author (cid:128) Project Page 2VinMotion Project lead Figure 1. HEAVE-HO enables decentralized humanoid teams to complete long-horizon collaborative tasks. Each robot acts on its own observations, the leaders planner chooses the next team skill and speaks it, and followers execute it in synchrony without any network communication. Videos can be found on our project page.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce HEAVE-HO, decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multihumanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop multi-agent post-training framework that adapts humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train vision-language planner and design speech-based leaderfollower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-BENCH, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 210 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that HEAVE-HO consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks. 1. Introduction Learning-based whole-body control has made individual humanoids increasingly capable [27, 42, 77, 78]. However, many tasks in homes, warehouses, and construction sites remain beyond the physical capabilities of single robot. Handling large or heavy objects, such as tables, bed frames, and large boxes, often requires multiple humanoids to share the load and coordinate their motion. Collaboration therefore promises to overcome these physical limits. Realizing this promise involves three interdependent challenges. First, interaction is tightly coupled: forces transmitted through shared object make each robots balance and grasp depend on its partners actions. Second, long-horizon tasks require visually grounded planning of coordinated action sequences, such as reorienting the team and its shared load before passing through narrow doorway. Third, execution must be synchronized: mistimed lift or step can destabilize the shared load and the robots. These challenges become especially demanding under decentralized execution. centralized policy can use teamwide observations to jointly coordinate the robots actions and align their execution timing [9, 44, 45, 62]. However, its input context and joint action space grow with team size, so policies with fixed input and output dimensions require modification and often retraining when robots are added. Gathering team-wide observations also requires network communication at inference. shared decentralized policy can instead preserve the same per-robot observation and action interface as the team grows, but must coordinate from local observations alone. Our goal is to combine this scalability with tightly synchronized whole-body collaboration, without network communication. We introduce HEAVE-HO, decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid locomanipulation. At the low level, our multi-agent posttraining framework augments frozen humanoid foundation tracking model [42] with residual policy shared across robots. We train this policy with multi-agent reinforcement learning using centralized critic and shared actor, while each robot relies only on local observations at execution. The resulting controller executes lifting, stepping, and turning skills with compatible start and end configurations, enabling their composition into long-horizon behaviors. At the high level, we train vision-language planner to select the next team skill from leader robots visual observations. speech-based leaderfollower mechanism aligns skill decisions and execution timing without network communication: the leader announces skill, followers recognize it locally, and all robots begin on shared execution schedule. The leader role can be assigned to any robot in the team, and the same speech interface allows person to follow commands or act as the leader. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce HHBENCH, benchmark of 12 collaborative tasks for teams of 210 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. The tasks span lifting and carrying, shoulder carrying, pulling, pushing, handover, and precise placement under spatial constraints such as narrow doors and corridors. Collaborative skills and task stages can be chained into long-horizon tasks. Across these tasks, our low-level policy succeeds in 94% of simulated episodes, compared with at most 29% for baseline and ablated controllers. Our planner completes 43 of 50 long-horizon trials, compared with 21 for zero-shot GPT-6 (Astra), while reducing per-decision latency by factor of about 120. Without retraining, the policy learned with two identical humanoids scales to teams of up to ten robots and collaborates with different humanoid platform and with people. Extensive real-world experiments further demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration on long-horizon tasks. Videos of the real-world and simulated experiments are provided on the project page. In summary, our contributions are: multi-agent post-training framework that adapts frozen humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled collaboration through shared residual policy, for decentralized control from local observations. trained vision-language model for coherent longhorizon planning, together with speech-based leader follower coordination mechanism for synchronized decentralized execution without network communication. HH-BENCH, benchmark of 12 collaborative tasks for teams of 210 humanoids, accompanied by systematic evaluations of scalability, heterogeneous collaboration, and real-world deployment. 2. Related Work Humanoid whole-body control and loco-manipulation. Learning-based methods have substantially advanced humanoid locomotion and athletic control [23, 35, 54, 55, 68, 78, 80]. To broaden these capabilities, motion imitation provides scalable route to acquiring diverse wholebody skills from human demonstrations [10, 11, 20, 25 28, 32, 38, 74, 75]. SONIC [42] further scales motion tracking into generalist controller with unified interface for teleoperation and general tracking. Recent work extends motion tracking to contact-rich interaction using motion capture data [47, 70, 77] or human videos [2, 65, 67]. Despite this progress, these methods primarily focus on the capabilities of individual humanoids. Our work adapts frozen foundation tracking model [42] through multiagent residual learning, enabling physically coupled multihumanoid loco-manipulation collaboration with decentralized control from local observations alone. Centralized and decentralized multi-robot collaboration. Centralized policies jointly process team observations and predict actions for multiple robots, supporting multi-arm manipulation [63, 64], collaborative legged pushing [46], and collaboration among heterogeneous robots [79]. Decentralized approaches learn coordinated policies through multi-agent reinforcement learning with centralized training and decentralized execution [41, 72] or joint imitation learning with diffusion policies and consensus representations [15, 24]. CHORUS [16] further extends this direction to shared pretrained vision-language-action model, enabling heterogeneous mobile manipulators to act independently from their own observations. Closely related to our setting, decPLM [50] learns decentralized pinch 2 liftmove control for quadrupedarm teams, assuming externally specified contact locations, synchronized initiation, and payload motion commands. In humanoid settings, existing work primarily investigates collaboration with human partners [4, 18, 36, 76]. Cooperative manipulation among multiple simulated characters has also been explored, which is confined to simulation only [21, 39, 71]. Our work targets autonomous long-horizon collaborative loco-manipulation by real humanoid teams, combining decentralized wholebody control with visually grounded skill planning and synchronized execution without network communication. Vision-language task planning. Language and visionlanguage models support long-horizon robot tasks by selecting and composing skills [1, 17, 30, 31] or generating executable control programs [37]. At the execution level, vision-language-action models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions [57, 22, 34, 48, 53, 66]. Hierarchical frameworks connect these levels by coupling task reasoning with learned visuomotor policies [60] or humanoid motion and skill controllers [14, 69, 73]. For robot teams, centralized language planners allocate tasks using team-level information [33, 40], while decentralized and hybrid planning frameworks coordinate robot-specific agents through explicit inter-agent dialogue [9, 44], which need network communication. In contrast, HEAVE-HO coordinates physically coupled humanoids without inter-robot network communication: trained vision-language planner selects shared team skills from the leaders local visual observations, and speech-based coordination synchronizes their execution. shared low-level policy realizes each skill through decentralized whole-body control using only each robots local observations. 3. Method 3.1. Overview We consider team of humanoids manipulating shared object. We call the team decentralized in strict sense: every robot acts only on its own observations, and no network message is exchanged between robots during task. The low-level policy runs on each robots on-board computer. Agent therefore observes only its proprioception, short window of its own future reference motion, and the object specification = (L, W, H, m) (length, width, height, and mass); it has no access to its partners states, and their actions affect it only through forces transmitted by the shared object. HEAVE-HO operates at two levels  (Fig. 2)  . The two levels communicate through vocabulary of team skills K, such as lift, put down, step in each direction, and rotation in place. The high level decides which team skill comes next, every few seconds, and makes sure that all robots start it together. The low level turns the current team skill into whole-body motion on every robot at 50 Hz. Each robot maps team skill to its own frame through fixed role map ρi : K; for two robots facing each other across box, moving the team toward the leaders front is forward step for the leader and backward step for its partner, whereas lifting and rotating are the same for both. 3.2. Low Level: Multi-Agent Post-Training Composable team skills. Every team skill starts and ends at one of two static hub poses: S0, standing empty-handed, and S1, standing while holding the object. Lift moves the team from S0 to S1, put down returns it to S0, and steps and rotations keep it at S1. Because all skills share these endpoints, any skill can follow any other, and long-horizon behavior reduces to sequence of discrete choices. Skills are defined at the team level: all robots start and end every skill in one canonical team layout and follow one common displacement profile during move, so the spacing between partners stays constant over long sequences. Steps have fixed length and rotations fixed angle, so the planner can reason about distance in units of skills, and when no new skill arrives the team simply holds its hub pose. Reference motions. We obtain references from two sources. We record pairs of people performing the task, recover their motion from video [59], and retarget it to the robots; we also generate references procedurally with inverse kinematics, which adds objects and interaction modes without new recordings. All references are cut into hub-tohub skills and conditioned on c: hand spread, grasp height, squat depth, and partner spacing adapt to the object, while the leg motion of each step is shared across objects. Residual post-training. Learning balance and locomotion from scratch under multi-agent coupling is sampleinefficient and fragile. We freeze foundation tracking model [42] as base policy πbase, which maps proprioception and reference to joint targets, and learn residual policy πθ that observes and corrects the base action: ai = πbase(oi) + πθ (cid:0)oi, πbase(oi)(cid:1). (1) The base policy provides balance and stepping, and the residual learns the forces and contacts needed to share load with partners. Exploration starts with small action noise, so early rollouts stay close to the base policy. Multi-agent reinforcement learning. All agents share the parameters θ of one actor [12], which keeps the policy independent of the team size. We train with multi-agent PPO [58, 72] under centralized training and decentralized execution [19, 41]: centralized critic Vϕ(s) RN receives the observations of all agents, concatenated in fixed agent order, and outputs one value per agent, of which agent uses the i-th entry, while each actor acts only on its own Figure 2. Overview of HEAVE-HO. At the high level, the leaders vision-language planner selects the next team skill from its camera and speaks it; every follower recognizes the command on board, and all robots start it on shared skill schedule. At the low level, each robot maps the team skill to its own role, generates reference conditioned on the object specification, and tracks it with frozen foundation tracking model plus residual policy shared by all robots. No network message is exchanged between robots. observation. Rewards are computed per agent and measure how well the agent tracks its own reference and how well the object follows its reference relative to the agent, with contact term that rewards keeping the hands loaded while carrying and gait term that rewards foot clearance and air time and penalizes dragging the feet. Terminations are coupled: when any agent fails, the episode ends for the whole team, so all agents are trained under shared outcome. selects them, and we collect 1,000 episodes for each task with initial positions sampled over wide range. single decision maker gives the team one coherent plan, which independent planners on each robot cannot guarantee. The planner can run on any computer that only the leader is connected to, since it never exchanges information with the other robots, and it is optional: without it, person can act as the leader. Training for composition and generalization. The skill is encoded only in the reference, so one network executes every skill and transitions never switch controllers. To cover all transitions, we train on long random chains of legal skills with balanced directions and random waiting times at the hubs, and initialize episodes at random points of these chains [51]. The object specification is an explicit input; during training the true size varies by 10% and the mass by 20% around the nominal value given to the policy, so single network adapts its grasp and posture to different objects. We further randomize friction, robot properties, and external pushes, and apply curricula on actuation delay and on the object tracking tolerance [52, 61]. 3.3. High Level: Planning and Synchronization Vision-language planner. leader decides the next team skill with vision-language model. Given the leaders headcamera image and the task instruction, the model outputs one token from {HOLD, DONE}. It is queried after each skill completes, so every decision is made from view of the team at rest, and long-horizon task unfolds as sequence of such decisions  (Fig. 3)  . We fine-tune Qwen3-VL2B [3] with LoRA [29] (settings in App. D.1) on episodes in which the leaders image is recorded whenever team skill is committed. In the real world, an operator selects the skills through the same interface, and we collect 24 episodes for each task of Sec. 5.3; in simulation, scripted planner Speech-based leader-follower synchronization. Starting skill together is critical: late lift tilts the object, and lone step pulls partner off balance. We separate what the team does from when it does it. What is decided once, by the leader. When is fixed by shared skill schedule: skill may only start on coarse grid of control ticks, so robots that learn about the same skill at slightly different moments still start it together. The decision is single discrete token, which the leader speaks through its speaker; every follower recognizes it with its on-board microphone, and every robot schedules the skill on the next slot of the grid, with the leader offsetting its own start by the expected acoustic delay. Because the grid is coarser than the variation in acoustic delay, this variation does not change the start slot, and the team starts every skill together without exchanging single packet. The leader is role rather than fixed robot, since every robot can host the same planner, and speech lets people join the team: person can follow the spoken skills or take over as leader. 3.4. Teams beyond Training Nothing in the low-level policy depends on the number of partners: it is shared, its inputs are egocentric, and partners enter only through the object. To deploy robots, we assign each robot slot around the object, which defines its reference and contact targets, and run the same policy on all of them; four robots carrying table, for instance, form 4 Team scaling and heterogeneity. The table carry suits larger teams: long table leaves room for many robots along its edges. Any robot can be replaced by person who follows the spoken skills, or by humanoid with different body; Secs. 5.2 and 5.5 report the teams we evaluate. Diverse interaction modes. Beyond lifting with the hands, the benchmark includes carrying palanquin or steel bar on the shoulders, pulling fire hose, pushing box or millstone, and handing box down from robot on higher level to partner below, who must take over the load at different height. In our setup, the higher level is the bed of truck, and the robot holding the box starts at different depths inside the truck and must first walk to its edge. These tasks change where the contacts are and how force is shared, while all robots must still act together. Composing long-horizon tasks. Because every task is executed as sequence of hub-to-hub team skills, tasks can be chained into longer ones. For example, two robots carry box up flight of stairs onto an elevated platform and place it on wheeled dolly; one of them then leaves its partner, walks to the edge of the platform, and hands second box of different size down to third robot standing below. Such compositions test whether the team stays coordinated across stages that use different skills, and whether robot can leave one team and join another within one task. Inputs and evaluation. Robots use only on-board sensing and the nominal object specification; motion capture and network communication between robots are not allowed. We report the success rate over 10 trials per task for real-world experiments and planners, and over three seeds of 512 teams for low-level controllers in simulation (Sec. 5.4). In simulation, the initial positions of the robots and the object are sampled over wide range that covers both easy and hard configurations, whereas real-world trials start from nominal configuration with small perturbations. Success rates in simulation and in the real world are therefore not directly comparable. trial succeeds if the team completes the task and reaches the target location without dropping the object. 5. Experiments We evaluate HEAVE-HO on HH-BENCH and answer four questions. (Q1) Can decentralized humanoid teams complete long-horizon collaborative tasks in the real world without communication? (Q2) Does the high-level planner choose better team skills than alternative decision makers? (Q3) How does the post-trained low-level policy compare with baseline controllers, and which of its design choices matter? (Q4) Does policy trained with two identical humanoids generalize to larger and heterogeneous teams? Figure 3. Leaders head-camera views over task, each with the team skill chosen at that step: the narrow door in the real world (top) and the box handover in simulation (bottom). two facing pairs side by side along its long edge. Partners that do not run the G1 policy join through the same skill interface: person follows the spoken skills, and humanoid with different body executes them with its own controller trained with the same recipe. 4. HH-BENCH: Multi-Humanoid Benchmark Evaluations of humanoid loco-manipulation mostly consider single robot, and multi-agent benchmarks [8, 57] rarely involve whole-body contact with shared object. There is thus no common testbed for humanoid teams that are physically coupled through shared object, where the balance and grasp of each robot depend on its partners. HHBENCH collects 12 collaborative tasks in which team of humanoids must act on the same object at the same time, often over long sequences of coordinated skills. The tasks differ in how the robots interact with the object (lifting and carrying, carrying on the shoulder, pulling, pushing, handing over, and precise placement) and in how the environment constrains the motion (Fig. 4; App. B.1 lists all tasks). No task prescribes team: each can be performed by teams of different sizes, including people and other humanoid platforms, in simulation or in the real world. Together they test the three requirements of collaboration: tightly coupled whole-body interaction, coherent long-horizon planning, and synchronized execution. Constrained transport. The narrow door is the signature task: the door is narrower than the object along its carrying direction, so the team first rotates the object in place and then walks through, with one robot moving forward and its partner backward. team that only walks along fixed direction cannot solve it. In the L-shaped corridor the team combines straight and sideways steps and must decide when to change direction while the robots and the object stay clear of the walls. Carrying an L-shaped sofa onto target area marked on the floor adds an irregular object whose load is distributed unevenly between the robots. Precise placement requires the team to place box within target region, which calls for the richest set of gaits: walking forward, backward, and sideways, and turning in place. 5 Figure 4. The tasks of HH-BENCH in simulation. Bottom: tasks can be chained into longer ones, here stair carry, placement on dolly, and handover of second box to third robot. Time sequences are in App. B.2 and videos on the project page. 5.1. Setup We use Unitree G1 humanoids with head-mounted stereo camera, and an EngineAI PM01 for heterogeneous teams. The PM01 runs its own policy trained with the same recipe. Policies run on each robots on-board computer at 50 Hz and are trained in Isaac-based simulation [43, 49] with 4,096 parallel two-robot environments [56]. 5.2. Real-World Collaboration Figure 5 shows real-world experiments of HEAVE-HO. Every robot runs the shared low-level policy on its own onboard computer, and no network message is exchanged between robots during task. Two-robot teams pass through the narrow door, follow the L-shaped corridor, hand box down from truck, and place box within target region. person can also take the place of one robot, carrying box through the narrow door or up flight of stairs together with G1. Finally, the two-robot policy is deployed to larger and heterogeneous teams that carry table (Sec. 5.5). person on the team can also take over as the leader and speak the team skills, as we do in some of these experiments. Every skill must start on all partners together, since late lift tilts the object and lone step pulls partner off balance. The videos on the project page show the spoken commands and the synchronized start of each skill. Across all tasks, the teams succeed in 92 of 100 trials (App. C.1 lists every team). Stair carry is the hardest (7/10): each step leaves room for little more than one foot, so small errors in foot placement are not tolerated. 5.3. High-Level Planning We evaluate the full system with different decision makers on five long-horizon tasks, with 10 trials per task (Tab. 1 and Fig. 6a). Two run in the real world: the narrow door and the L-shaped corridor. Three run in simulation: box handover from the bed of truck, in which the robot holding the box starts at different depths inside the truck and must walk to its edge before handing the box down; carrying long table with four robots to the front of sofa; and placing an L-shaped sofa on target area marked on the floor. We compare our fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-2B planner against two strong baselines: (1) zero-shot GPT-6 (Astra) with the same skill interface, and (2) CHORUS [16], decentralized policy executed independently on each robot. We fine-tune CHORUS on the same data following its recipe, including the π0.5 backbone [53], LoRA adapters, and fixed identity prompt per robot, and change only its output: instead of action chunks, it selects team skills like our planner, which isolates the coordination problem. An operator who selects the team skills manually serves as the upper bound. Our planner matches the operator on all three simulated tasks and approaches it on the two real-world tasks, whereas GPT-6 (Astra) used zero-shot fails far more often on every 6 Figure 5. Real-world experiments. The first four rows show two G1 robots over time, from left to right, labeled with the team skill being executed. The last row shows teams that differ from the training configuration, including different humanoid and people. Faces are obscured for anonymity. Full time sequences of all teams are in App. C.2 and videos on the project page. task. Our planner is also the fastest: one decision takes 52.5 ms on single RTX 4090 GPU with 5.3 GiB of memory, compared with 78 ms for CHORUS and 6.46 on average for GPT-6 (Astra) through its API, about 120 times longer. CHORUS fails every trial on all tasks except the handover, where it succeeds in 6 of 10 trials. Each robot runs its own copy of the policy and advances through its actions asynchronously, with no mechanism to align when the robots act [16]. The copies on different robots therefore start their skills at different moments, which breaks tasks in which the robots carry an object together. The handover couples the robots only briefly: one robot carries the box to the trucks edge, and its partner approaches to receive it, which leaves CHORUS some chance of success. 5.4. Low-Level Post-Training For each task, we compare the low-level policy against two baselines and two ablations in simulation, using the same skill chains, objects, and randomization (Tab. 2). Body and object errors are mean position errors over the full reference horizon, including frames after failure. Per-task results are in App. E.1. from HEAVE-HO and learns the full action with the same multi-agent setup. Independent actors gives each agent its own actor instead of sharing parameters, while keeping the centralized critic. Table 2 and Fig. 6b report the results. HEAVE-HO succeeds in 94.41% of the episodes on average, while no other controller exceeds 28.56%. Pure SONIC tracks the body reference more closely than Multi-HDMI and HEAVE-HO w/o SONIC but almost never completes task: the foundation tracker reproduces the motion, yet does not know how to exert force on the object or share the load with its partners. Without SONIC, learning the full whole-body action from scratch gives the largest body error and succeeds almost only on the two pushing tasks, which do not require lifting the object. Starting from the frozen tracker instead, the residual only needs to refine tracking and interaction. Independent actors reach 22.05%. With shared actor, every update draws on the experience of all agents, which face similar but not identical situations in collaborative task, and the number of parameters does not grow with the team size. Multi-HDMI succeeds mainly on shoulder carry and pushing, and fails on tightly coupled lifting, where critic that sees only local observations cannot tell how the partner contributes. Figure 7. Train with two, deploy with many. The policy trained with two G1 robots (top left) carries table in simulation with teams of four, eight, and ten robots, without retraining. 5.5. Train with Two, Deploy with Many All G1 policies are trained with exactly two identical robots. We deploy the same policy, without retraining, to teams that differ from this configuration in size and in composition. In the real world  (Fig. 5)  , four G1 robots carry table as two pairs side by side, three G1 robots carry it with person, G1 carries it with person and PM01, and PM01 carries it with person; these teams succeed in 37 of 40 trials. In simulation, the same policy drives teams of four, eight, and ten G1 robots carrying table  (Fig. 7)  . Two properties make this possible: the shared actor has no notion of team size, and partners affect each robot only through the object. Parameter sharing is essential, since independent actors would require new actor for every additional robot. 6. Conclusion introduced HEAVE-HO, We decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid locomanipulation. At the low level, multi-agent post-training turns frozen humanoid foundation tracking model into shared controller for physically coupled whole-body inter8 action. At the high level, vision-language planner gives the team one coherent long-horizon plan, more accurately and about 120 times faster than GPT-6 (Astra) used zeroshot, and speech-based leader-follower mechanism executes it in synchrony without network communication. On HH-BENCH, HEAVE-HO completes long-horizon collaborative tasks in the real world, and policy trained with two identical humanoids carries over to teams of up to ten robots, to different humanoid platform, and to people. Limitations. Synchronization relies on followers hearing the leader, so it requires reasonably quiet environment and reliable sound pickup. Training the planner for new task requires demonstrations collected manually by teleoperation, which is time-consuming.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: Task Team Success A. Human Participants The people who appear in our real-world experiments, figures, and videos are members of the research team and are among the authors. They took part as carrying partners or as the leader who speaks the team commands. No data about the participants themselves was collected or analyzed, and the evaluation measures only task success; therefore, no IRB review was sought. All participants consented to appear in the figures and videos, and their faces are obscured to preserve anonymity. B. Benchmark Details B.1. Tasks Table 3 lists the 12 tasks of HH-BENCH, grouped by how the robots interact with the object; Fig. 4 shows each of them in simulation. Task What it tests Lift and carry L-shaped corridor Narrow door Table carry L-shaped sofa Stair carry Precise placement Handover Box handover Shoulder carry Palanquin Rebar Pull Fire hose Push Box push Millstone steps along turning path rotating to fit through door large object shared by many robots an irregular, unevenly loaded object partners at different heights placing box in target region passing load down to partner load carried above the arms long load along line of robots pulling deformable object pushing heavy object together pushing around fixed axis Table 3. Tasks in HH-BENCH, grouped by how the robots interact with the object. B.2. Simulated Time Sequences Figures 10 and 11 show time sequence for each of the 12 tasks, in the order of Tab. 3. C. Figure 9 shows the full time sequences of these other teams, together with the team of three G1 robots and person, which is listed in Tab. 4 but not shown in Fig. 5. D. Implementation Details D.1. Planner Training Table 5 lists the training settings of the vision-language planner described in Sec. 3.3. Item Value LoRA targets (vision) Base model LoRA rank / alpha LoRA targets (LLM) Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct 32 / 64 q, k, v, o, gate, up, and down projections in every layer attention qkv and output projections and both MLP layers in the last 8 ViT blocks fully trained Vision merger Trainable parameters 140 (4.2 in the ViT LoRA) Optimizer Learning rate Batch size AdamW, 5% warmup, cosine decay 2 104 (LLM), 5 105 (ViT) 4 4 gradient accumulation (effective 16) 2 bf16 base weights, fp32 trainable parameters, gradient checkpointing 24 real-world episodes or 1,000 simulated episodes per task 52.5 ms per decision, 5.3 GiB, one RTX 4090 GPU Epochs Precision Training data Inference Table 5. Training settings of the vision-language planner. 13 E. Additional Results E.1. Per-Task Low-Level Results Section 5.4 compares the low-level controllers averaged over the 12 tasks of HH-BENCH (Tab. 2) and shows their success rate on each task (Fig. 6b). Table 7 lists the success rate, body error, and object error of every controller on each task. F. Supplementary Videos All videos are on the project page. The webpage contains summary video; the spoken team commands with sound, with either robot or person as the leader; videos of all real-world experiments in Tab. 4; and videos of the tasks in HH-BENCH in simulation, including long-horizon task composed of several of them. Figure 8. Head camera mount. (a) ZED stereo camera on the head of G1. (b, c) The two 3D-printed parts of the mount. D.2. Low-Level Policy Training We post-train the low-level policy in Isaac Lab with teams of two Unitree G1 robots. shared actor predicts jointtarget residuals on top of frozen SONIC, and centralized critic sees the concatenated observations of both robots during training. We train teacher with privileged simulator observations and distill its mean actions into student while training an adaptation module to predict the privileged latent from local inputs. We then fine-tune the student with MAPPO in closed loop. Both teacher and student use the same frozen SONIC base. Table 6 gives the MAPPO settings. For the box-carrying skills (lifting, putting down, stepping in each direction, and turning in place), which together cover the two-robot box-carrying tasks such as the narrow door and the L-shaped corridor, and for the box handover, training uses 4,096 parallel teams and budget of 109 environment steps per training stage, counting one step per team.
